nodes.name: null expansion / null mean curvature $\theta^+_{\Sigma_t}$
nodes.statement: The quantity $H+P$ corresponds to the {\it null expansion} or \textit{null mean curvature} $\theta_{\Sigma_t}^+$ of $\Sigma_t$ with respect to its future directed outward null vector field $l^+:=\nu+\vec{n}$, \begin{equation*} \theta^+_{\Sigma_t}:=\langle\vec{H}_{\Sigma_t},l^+\rangle_h=H+P, \end{equation*} where $\vec{H}_{\Sigma_t}$, the mean curvature vector of $\Sigma_t$ inside the spacetime $L$, is given by \begin{equation*}\vec{H}_{\Sigma_t}:=H\nu-P\vec{n}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The null expansion $\theta^+_{\Sigma_t}$ is the pairing of the spacetime mean curvature vector with the outward null field, and equals $H+P$.
differentia: with respect to its future directed outward null vector field $l^+:=\nu+\vec{n}$

nodes.name: marginally outer trapped hypersurface (MOTS)
nodes.statement: If $\theta_{\Sigma}^+$ vanishes on all of $\Sigma$, then $\Sigma$ is called a \textit{marginally outer trapped hypersurface}, or MOTS for short.
nodes.origin_citation: standard notion in general relativity; the paper refers to \cite{AMS08, AM09, AM10}

nodes.name: $C$-minimizing current / $(C,1)$-minimal set
nodes.statement: In the language of {\it currents} or of {\it finite perimeter sets} (codimension 1), the bound on the mean curvature implies that $N_k$ is a {\it $C$-minimizing current} (see \cite{DS93}) or a {\it $(C, 1)$-minimal set} (see \cite{MaMi}), i.e. that \[\mass(N_k)\le \mass(N_k+\partial Q)+C\mass(Q), \forall (n+1)\text{-current }Q.\]
nodes.statement_short: A current whose mass beats any competitor up to an additive $C\,\mass(Q)$ penalty; the mean-curvature bound puts $N_k$ in this class.
nodes.genus: currents or of {\it finite perimeter sets} (codimension 1)

nodes.name: reaction-diffusion equation for the null mean curvature $H+P$
nodes.statement_short: Evolution equation for $H+P$ under the flow, with a cubic reaction term forcing finite-time singularities.

nodes.name: steepest descent identity for area plus bulk energy
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} \frac{d}{dt}\left(|\Sigma_t|+\int_{V_t}P dV\right)=-\int_{\Sigma_t} H(H+P) + P(H+P)d\mu=-\int_{\Sigma_t} (H+P)^2 d\mu, \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Null mean curvature flow is the $L^2$ steepest descent flow of area plus bulk energy $P$.

nodes.name: Harnack-type differential inequality for the vertical component $1/v$

nodes.statement_short: Differential inequality for the vertical component of the normal, the input to the Hopf maximum principle in the blow-up analysis.

nodes.name: Main theorem (existence of weak solutions blowing up on the outermost MOTS)
nodes.statement: Let $(M^{n+1},g,K)$ be an initial data set for a space-time, and let $\partial\Omega_{\out}=\Sigma_{\out}$ denote the outermost MOTS in $M$. Let $\Omega$ be a smooth domain in $M$ with $\Omega_\out\subset\Omega$, and whose boundary, $\partial\Omega$, is a mean convex closed and bounded outer trapped embedded hypersurface in $M$. Then for $2\le n\le 6$ the following hold: \begin{enumerate}[(i)] \item Let $\lambda=\max_i\{|\l_i|, \l_i\text{  eigenvalue of  } K\}$. Then, for any $0<\e\le \min\left\{\frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda}, \frac12\right\}$ there exists a solution $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}\in C^\infty(\Omega\setminus\Omega_\out)$ of the equation $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon}})$ that is zero on $\partial\Omega$ and blows up to infinity over $\Sigma_\out$, that is $\lim_{x\to x_0}\hat u_\e(x)=\infty$ for any $x_0\in \Sigma_\out$. \item There exists a sequence of $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon_k}$ as in (i) with $\e_k\downarrow 0$ such that $u_{\e_k}\to u$ in $C^0(\Omega_1\cup\partial \Omega)$, where $u\in C^{0,1}(\Omega_1\cup\partial\Omega)$ and $\Omega_1\subset \Omega\setminus \Omega_\out$ is such that $\partial\Omega\subset\partial\Omega_1$ and $\partial^* (\Omega\setminus\Omega_1)$ is a {\it generalized} MOTS (see Definition~\ref{weakMOTS} and Remark~\ref{weakrmk}). \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For $2\le n\le 6$, solutions of the regularized problem exist and blow up exactly on the outermost MOTS, and their limit is a weak solution converging to a generalized MOTS.

nodes.name: Limit as $\kappa\to0$: blow-up over a MOTS
nodes.statement: Assume that $2\le n\le 6$ and let $(M^{n+1},g,K)$ be an initial data set and let $\partial\Omega$ be a smooth, strictly mean convex and outer untrapped hypersurface in $M$. Then, for $\e\le \min\left\{\frac{1}{(n+1)\lambda},\frac12\right\}$, where $\lambda=\max_i\{|\l_i|, \l_i\text{  eigenvalue of  } K\}$, there exists a sequence $\{\k_i\}_{i\in\N}$ with $\kappa_i\downarrow0$, together with an open and connected set $\Omega_\e$ such that if $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon,\k_i}$ solves $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon},\k_i})$ the following hold. $(i)$ The sequence $\{\hat{u}_{\varepsilon, \k_i}\}_{i\in\N}$ converges uniformly to $+\infty$ on $\partial\Omega_\e\setminus \partial \Omega$, and $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon,\k_i}$ converges locally smoothly to $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}$ in $\Omega_\e$, where $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}$ is a smooth function that satisfies $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon}})$ in ${\Omega}_\e$. $(ii)$ Each boundary component $\Sigma_{\e}$ of $\partial \Omega_\e\setminus\partial\Omega$ is an embedded MOTS satisfying $\theta^+_{\Sigma_\e}=H_{\Sigma_{\e}}+{\tr}_{\Sigma_{\e}}K=0$, where $H_{\Sigma_{\e}}$ is the mean curvature of $\Sigma_\e$ taken with respect to the inward pointing unit normal to $\Omega_\e$. $(iii)$ If $\Omega$ does not contain a closed MOTS in its interior, $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon,\k_i}$ converges to a smooth solution $\hat{u}_{\varepsilon}$ of $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon}})$ defined on all of $\bar{\Omega}$.

nodes.name: Blow-up over the outermost MOTS
nodes.statement: There exists an $\e_0$ depending only on the initial data, such that for any $\e\le \e_0$ the following holds. There exists a solution $\hat u_\e\in C^\infty(\Omega_0)$ of the equation ($*_{\hat\e}$), where $\Omega_0=\Omega\setminus\ov\Omega_\infty$, such that $\hat u_\e$ blows up over the inner boundary $\partial\Omega_0\setminus\partial\Omega=\Sigma_\out$ (the outermost MOTS) and is zero over the outer boundary $\partial \Omega$. Consequently the function $u_\e=\e\hat u_\e$ is then a smooth solution of ($*_{\e}$) in $\Omega_0$ that blows up over the inner boundary $\Sigma_\out$ (the outermost MOTS) and is zero over the outer boundary $\partial \Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: For small $\varepsilon$ the solution $\hat u_\e$ exists on $\Omega\setminus\ov\Omega_\infty$ and blows up precisely on the outermost MOTS.

nodes.statement: There exists $u\in C^{0,1}(\Omega_1\cup\partial\Omega)$ a weak solution of $(**)$, as in Definition~\ref{weak}, where $\Omega_1\stackrel{open}{\subset} (\Omega\setminus\ov\Omega_\out)$ and $\partial\Omega_1\supset\partial\Omega$ (recall that $\Omega_\out$ is such that $\partial\Omega_\out=\Sigma_\out$, the outermost MOTS). nodes.name: Weak solutions and the form of the outermost MOTS
nodes.statement: We will call a function $u$ as in (ii) of Theorem~\ref{MOTS} a weak solution of $(**)$ and its level sets $(\Sigma_t=\{u=t\})_{t\ge 0}$ a weak solution of $(*)$ (see Definition~\ref{weak}). Theorem~\ref{MOTS} (ii) then states that there exists a weak solution of $(*)$ with initial condition $\Sigma_0=\partial\Omega$, $(\Sigma_t)_{t\ge 0}$, that converges to a generalized MOTS that lies outside the outermost MOTS. Note also that the fact that the outermost MOTS has the form $\Sigma_\infty=\partial\Omega_\infty$, where $\Omega_\infty$ is an open set, is not an assumption---this is always the case with $\Omega_\infty$ being the union of all weakly outer trapped sets in $M$, that is open sets with weakly outer trapped boundary (i.e. satisfying $\theta^+\le 0$), as is shown in \cite{AM09}.
nodes.statement_short: Terminology for weak solutions, and the observation that the outermost MOTS is automatically the boundary of an open set.

nodes.name: The case of empty outermost MOTS

nodes.name: Regularity of generalized MOTS
nodes.statement: If $\partial^* E$ is a generalized MOTS, then by Allard's regularity theorem \cite{Al} (see also \cite{Alex}) we infer that, away from a set of $\H^n$-measure zero, $\partial^*E$ is a $C^{1,\a}$ hypersurface for any $\a\in (0,1)$. This implies that locally (away from a set of $\H^n$-measure zero) it is the graph of a function that satisfies equation \eqref{Jang} weakly, and using standard PDE methods we obtain that $\partial^* E$ is smooth, and thus a MOTS in the classical sense, away from a set of $\H^n$-measure zero. Furthermore, since the mean curvature is bounded on the reduced boundary, we also have that if $\partial^* E$ is a generalized MOTS then $\H^n(\partial E\setminus\partial^*E)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: By Allard's theorem a generalized MOTS is a smooth MOTS away from an $\H^n$-null set, and $\H^n(\partial E\setminus\partial^*E)=0$.

nodes.name: Roadmap of the proof of the main theorem
nodes.statement: The proof of the main theorem, Theorem~\ref{main}, is given in Theorems \ref{kto0}, \ref{blowup}, \ref{weak existence} and \ref{MOTSconv}. In Section \ref{properties}, we give various properties for the graphs of the functions $\hat u_\e$, $\hat u$, the most important being a minimizing property (see Lemmas \ref{emin}, \ref{eminu}). Furthermore, in addition to (locally) uniform convergence of the functions $\hat u_\e$ to $\hat u$, we obtain convergence, in the sense of varifolds, of their graphs (see Theorem~\ref{mainconvii}).

Local uniform area bound

nodes.name: Alternative variational definition of weak solutions and uniqueness
nodes.statement: Finally, we would like to remark that if the level $\{u=t\}$ minimize ``area $+\int \left(P-\frac{1}{|\nabla u|}\right)$'' then we can define a weak solution of $(*)$ using this minimization property, as was done in \cite{MS} for the mean curvature flow (see also \cite{HI01, KM13} for the inverse mean curvature flow and the inverse null mean curvature flow). In \cite{MS}, this definition was used to show that the level set flow is unique and it is not hard to check that the methods from \cite{MS} can be applied to our case to show uniqueness.
nodes.statement_short: A variational definition of weak solutions would give uniqueness of the level set flow, as in Metzger--Schulze.

nodes.name: Convergence of weak solutions to the outermost MOTS
nodes.statement: We believe that weak solutions $(\Sigma_t)_{t\ge0}$ (as in Remark~\ref{thmrmk}) actually converge to the outermost MOTS. However, as our proof yields only {\it weak} convergence of the $\Sigma_t$'s as $t\to \infty$, we can only deduce that the limit is a {\it generalized} MOTS. If the generalized limit can be shown to be regular, then, as it lies outside the outermost MOTS, the two must coincide.
nodes.statement_short: Do weak solutions converge to the outermost MOTS itself? Only convergence to a generalized MOTS is proved.

nodes.name: Regularity of the limit: is $V=0$ and $\partial^*E_\infty$ a classical MOTS?
nodes.statement: We believe that $V=0$ and $\partial^*E_\infty=\partial E_\infty$ is actually a MOTS in the classical sense and therefore, as it lies outside the outermost MOTS, it is indeed the outermost MOTS. Such a result would be concluded if we had some control over the singular set of null mean curvature flow, similar to that in \cite{W00} for mean curvature flow.
nodes.statement_short: Conjecturally the extra varifold piece $V$ vanishes and the limit is a classical (outermost) MOTS.

nodes.name: White-type regularity theory for null mean curvature flow
nodes.statement: Therefore, the question is how can we show the above convergence. It is not hard to check that the arguments from \cite{MS} apply in our case, provided that the regularity theory of White \cite{W00} for the mean curvature flow is also true in our case. In particular we would like to have the following: There exists a singular set $S\subset \graph u$ of parabolic Hausdorff dimension at most $n-1$ outside of which the sets $\{u=t\}$ are a smooth level set flow.

nodes.name: Proof of the Supremum estimate
nodes.statement: Since $\hat u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$, either $\hat{u}\leq0$ or $\hat{u}$ has an interior maximum. nodes.name: Proof of the Boundary gradient estimate
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the equation in level-set form, check the Gilbarg--Trudinger structure and boundary-curvature conditions, and apply Serrin's barrier construction.

nodes.name: Invoke Serrin's classical barrier construction
nodes.statement: Since $\partial\Omega$ is strictly mean convex and outer untrapped with respect to the outward pointing unit normal (so that on $\partial \Omega$ $H+sP>0$ for $s\in[0,1]$) we can use the classical barrier construction of Serrin, as presented in \cite[Theorem 14.6]{GT01}, to obtain the desired boundary gradient estimate.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Serrin's boundary gradient estimate, available because $H+sP>0$ on $\partial\Omega$.

nodes.name: Rewrite the equation in terms of the level sets
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $v^3$ to obtain the operator $Q$ adapted to the level sets rather than the graph.

nodes.statement: and decompose it, as in \cite[(14.43)]{GT01}, into the following coefficients \begin{align} Q\hat u&=(\Lambda a^{ij}_{\infty}+a^{ij}_0)\nabla_{ij}\hat{u}+|\nabla\hat{u}|\Lambda b_{\infty}+b_0=0, \end{align} where \[a^{ij}_{\infty}(x,z,p)=a^{ij}_{\infty}\left(x,\frac{p}{|p|}\right)=\left(g^{ij}-\frac{p^ip^j}{|p|^2}\right),\,\,a^{ij}_0=\frac{p^ip^j}{|p|^2},\,\,\Lambda=1+|p|^2,\] \[b_{\infty}(x,z,p)=b_{\infty}\left(x,z,\frac{p}{|p|}\right)=-sK_{ij}\left(g^{ij}-\frac{p^ip^j}{|p|^2}\right)-\kappa z\] and \[b_0=-\kappa z\frac{\Lambda}{\Lambda^{1/2}+|p|}-sK_{ij}\left(g^{ij}\frac{\Lambda}{\Lambda^{1/2}+|p|}+\frac{p^ip^j}{|p|}\frac{\Lambda^{1/2}}{\Lambda^{1/2}+|p|}\right)+\frac{s}{\varepsilon}\Lambda.\]

nodes.name: Verify the structure and boundary curvature conditions and conclude
nodes.statement_short: Check (14.50)-(14.51) of Gilbarg--Trudinger and apply their Theorem 14.6 to get the upper barrier.

nodes.name: Closedness of $I$ from the a-priori estimates

nodes.name: Proof of non-fattening
nodes.statement:
The proof is exactly as that of \cite[Lemma 5.5]{S08}, where the same result is proven in the case $P=0$. We repeat the main step here and sketch the rest of the proof, using the notation of Definition~ef{U}. Let $0<t_1<t_2$ and $\Omega_1'=\Omega_1	imes I$ for some interval $I=(a,b)$. By using the coarea formula, \eqref{MCet2}, H"older's inequality, Remark~ef{area bound}, and Lemma~ef{H+Pk}, we obtain \[ egin{split} |\H^{n+2}(\wt E_{t_1}^k\cap\Omega_1')-\H^{n+2}(\wt E_{t_2}^k\cap\Omega_1')|&=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\int_{\wt\Sigma^k_t\cap\Omega_1'}|H_t^k+P(
u_k)|\ &\le C|t_2-t_1|^ rac12, \end{split}\] where $C$ is a constant independent on $k$. Let now $S=\{t>0:\H^{n+2}\{U=t\}>0\}=\{t>0:\H^{n+1}\{u=t\}>0\}$ and note that for any $t
otin S$ $\wt E_t^k	o\wt E_t$ in $L^1_\loc$ (in the sense that their characteristic functions converge in $L^1_\loc(\Omega_1	imes\R)$), because of the local uniform convergence $U_{\e_k}	o U$ in $\Omega_1	imes\R$. Thus, for $t_1,t_2
otin S$, the limit of the above estimate yields \[|\H^{n+2}(\wt E_{t_1}\cap\Omega_1')-\H^{n+2}(\wt E_{t_2}\cap\Omega_1')|\le C|t_2-t_1|^ rac12.\] For any $t\in S$ (a countable set) we can now pick two sequences of times $t_1^j<t<t_2^j$ for which the above is true and such that both sequences tend to $t$. This then implies that $\H^{n+2}\{U=t\}=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Hölder continuity in $t$ of the volumes of $\wt E_t^k$ (from the $L^2$ bound on $H+P$) passes to the limit and squeezes the exceptional times.

We repeat the main step here and sketch the rest of the proof, using the notation of Definition~\ref{U}. Let $0<t_1<t_2$ and $\Omega_1'=\Omega_1\times I$ for some interval $I=(a,b)$. By using the coarea formula, \eqref{MCet2}, H\"older's inequality, Remark~\ref{area bound}, and Lemma~\ref{H+Pk}, we obtain \[\begin{split} |\H^{n+2}(\wt E_{t_1}^k\cap\Omega_1')-\H^{n+2}(\wt E_{t_2}^k\cap\Omega_1')|&=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\int_{\wt\Sigma^k_t\cap\Omega_1'}|H_t^k+P(\nu_k)|\\ &\le C|t_2-t_1|^\frac12, \end{split}\] where $C$ is a constant independent on $k$.

nodes.statement: Let now $S=\{t>0:\H^{n+2}\{U=t\}>0\}=\{t>0:\H^{n+1}\{u=t\}>0\}$ and note that for any $t\notin S$ $\wt E_t^k\to\wt E_t$ in $L^1_\loc$ (in the sense that their characteristic functions converge in $L^1_\loc(\Omega_1\times\R)$), because of the local uniform convergence $U_{\e_k}\to U$ in $\Omega_1\times\R$. Thus, for $t_1,t_2\notin S$, the limit of the above estimate yields \[|\H^{n+2}(\wt E_{t_1}\cap\Omega_1')-\H^{n+2}(\wt E_{t_2}\cap\Omega_1')|\le C|t_2-t_1|^\frac12.\]

nodes.statement: For any $t\in S$ (a countable set) we can now pick two sequences of times $t_1^j<t<t_2^j$ for which the above is true and such that both sequences tend to $t$. This then implies that $\H^{n+2}\{U=t\}=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximating any $t\in S$ from both sides forces $\H^{n+2}\{U=t\}=0$.

u)d\H^{n+2},\] where $\wt W=W	imes[-2\ell, 2\ell]$. This then yields \[ egin{split} 2\ell|\partial^* E_t\cap W|+2\ell \int_{ W\cap  E_t} P(
u)d\H^{n+1}\le& 2\ell|\partial^* F\cap  W|+2\H^{n+1}(F\setminus E_t)\ &+2\ell \int_{W\cap  F} P(
u)d\H^{n+1}. \end{split}\] Dividing by $\ell$ and letting $\ell	o \infty$ provides the required property.
nodes.statement_short: Compare $\wt E_t^k$ with the competitor $F^k=\wt E_t^k\cup(F\cap W)$, pass to the limit using traces, lower semicontinuity and the $L^2$ convergence of normals, then unwrap the product structure.

nodes.name: Normalize the competitor domain $W$
nodes.statement: The proof follows that of \cite[Lemma 5.6, Corollary 5.7]{S08}, where the same statements are proven in the case when $P=0$. Let $W$, $F$ be as in the statement of the lemma and note that $F\setminus\wt E_t\subset\Omega_1\times\R$. First, note that arguing exactly as in \cite[Lemma 5.6]{S08}, we can assume, by passing to a slightly larger compact set if necessary, that for $W$ the following is true. The boundary $\partial W$ is smooth, $|\partial^*(F\cup \wt E_t^k)\cap\partial W|=|\partial^*(F\cap \wt E_t^k)\cap\partial W|=|\partial^* \wt E_t^k\cap\partial W|=0$ for all $k$ and $\lim_{k\to\infty}\int_{\partial W} |\phi^-_{F\cup \wt E_t^k}-\phi^+_{\wt E_t^k}|d\H^{n+1}= 0$, where $\phi^-_{F\cup \wt E_t^k}$ and $\phi^+_{\wt E_t^k}$ are the inner and outer trace of ${F\cup \wt E_t^k}$ and $\wt E_t^k$ on $\partial W$ (see \cite[Chapter 2]{Giu} and \cite[Section 2.4]{Alex} for definitions of the traces and note that here we also use Remark~\ref{setconv}).
nodes.statement_short: Enlarge $W$ slightly so that its boundary is smooth and the traces converge.

nodes.name: Compare with the competitor $F^k$
nodes.statement: Let now $F^k= \wt E_t^k\cup (F\cap W)$. We then have \[\begin{split}|\partial^*F^k\cap W|=&\int_{\partial W} |\phi^-_{F\cup \wt E_t^k}-\phi^+_{\wt E_t^k}|d\H^{n+1}+|\partial^*(F\cup \wt E_t^k)\cap W|\\ =&\int_{\partial W} |\phi^-_{F\cup \wt E_t^k}-\phi^+_{\wt E_t^k}|d\H^{n+1}+ |\partial^* \wt E^k_t\cap W|\\ &+ |\partial^* F\cap W|-|\partial^*(F\cap \wt E_t^k)\cap W|, \end{split}\] where the second equality above is justified by arguing as in \cite[(36) of proof Lemma~5.6]{S08}). By the minimizing property of $\wt E_t^k$ (since $F^k\supset \wt E_t^k$), we have \[|\partial^* \wt E^k_t\cap W|-\int_{W\cap (F^k\setminus \wt E^k_t)} P(\nu_k)d\H^{n+2}\le |\partial^* F^k\cap W|,\] and thus we obtain \[\begin{split} |\partial^* F\cap W|\ge &|\partial^*(F\cap \wt E_t^k)\cap W|- \int_{W\cap (F^k\setminus \wt E^k_t)} P(\nu_k)d\H^{n+2}\\ &-\int_{\partial W} |\phi^-_{F\cup \wt E_t^k}-\phi^+_{\wt E_t^k}|d\H^{n+1}. \end{split}\]
nodes.statement_short: Apply the minimizing property of $\wt E_t^k$ to $F^k=\wt E_t^k\cup(F\cap W)$.

nodes.name: Reduce to convergence of the bulk energy terms
nodes.statement:
Since the last term on the right-hand side vanishes as $k	o \infty$ and $|\partial^* \wt E_t\cap W|=|\partial^*(F\cap \wt E_t)\cap W| \le \lim_{k	o\infty}|\partial^*(F\cap\wt E_t^k)\cap W|$ (by Remark~ef{setconv} and the lower semi-continuity, see \cite[Theorem 1.9]{Giu} and \cite[Theorem 2.38]{Alex}), it suffices to show that \[\int_{W\cap (F^k\setminus \wt E^k_t)} P(
u_k)d\H^{n+2} \stackrel{k	o \infty}{\longrightarrow}\int_{W\cap (F\setminus \wt E_t)} P(
u)d\H^{n+2}, \] where $
u$ is as in the statement of the lemma. To see this, we note that $W\cap (F^k\setminus \wt E^k_t)=(F\cap W)\setminus\wt E_t^k$ and $ W\cap (F\setminus \wt E_t)=(F\cap W)\setminus \wt E_t$, and we write \[ egin{split}\int_{W\cap (F^k\setminus \wt E^k_t)} &P(
u_k)d\H^{n+2}-\int_{W\cap (F\setminus \wt E_t)} P(
u)d\H^{n+2} \ =& \int_{W\cap F\cap(\wt E_t\setminus\wt E_t^k)} P(
u_k)d\H^{n+2}-\int_{W\cap F\cap(\wt E^k_t\setminus\wt E_t)} P(
u_k)d\H^{n+2}\ &+ \int_{W\cap (F\setminus \wt E_t)} P(
u_k)-P(
u)d\H^{n+2}. \end{split}\]
nodes.statement_short: By lower semicontinuity it suffices to show the $P(\nu_k)$ integrals converge.

nodes.name: Prove the two convergences
nodes.statement:
We can see now that the right-hand side of the above equality tends to $0$, as $k	o \infty$, because of the fact that $P$ is bounded, Remark~ef{setconv} and Lemma~ef{ES conv}. More specifically, we have the following two observations. First, by Remark~ef{setconv}, we have \[\H^{n+2}(W\cap (\wt E_t\setminus \wt E^k_t))\,,\,\, \H^{n+2}(W\cap (\wt E_t^k\setminus \wt E_t))\stackrel{k	o \infty}{\longrightarrow} 0,\] which implies that the first two terms tend to zero. Second, by Lemma~ef{ES conv} (see also Remark~ef{ES conv2}), we have \[\int_{W\cap (F\setminus \wt E_t)} 
u_k^i-
u^id\H^{n+2}\le C(W)\|
u_k-
u\|_{L^2(W)} \stackrel{k	o \infty}{\longrightarrow}0,\] and thus, by writing $
u_k^i
u_k^j-
u^i
u^j=
u_k^i(
u_k^j-
u^j)+
u^j(
u_k^i-
u^i)$, we have \[\int_{W\cap (F\setminus \wt E_t)} 
u_k^i
u_k^j-
u^i
u^jd\H^{n+2}\stackrel{k	o \infty}{\longrightarrow}0.\] Since $P(
u_k)- P(
u)= (
u_k^i
u_k^j-

nodes.statement_short: Set convergence kills the first two terms; $L^2$ convergence of the normals kills the third.

nodes.name: Unwrap the product structure to get the property for $E_t$
nodes.statement:
Finally, one can easily see that the same minimization property holds for $E_t$ in $\Omega_1$ as follows (cf. \cite[Corollary 5.7]{S08}). Let $W\subset \Omega$ be a compact set and let $F$ be a finite perimeter set such that $E_t\subset F$ and $F\setminus E_t\subset W$. Given any $\ell>0$, let $\wt F=(F	imes(-\ell,\ell))\cup \wt E_t$. Using the minimization property of $\wt E_t$, we have \[|\partial^*\wt E_t\cap \wt W|+\int_{\wt W\cap \wt E_t} P(
u)d\H^{n+2}\le |\partial^*\wt F\cap \wt W|+\int_{\wt W\cap \wt F} P(
u)d\H^{n+2},\] where $\wt W=W	imes[-2\ell, 2\ell]$. This then yields \[ egin{split} 2\ell|\partial^* E_t\cap W|+2\ell \int_{ W\cap  E_t} P(
u)d\H^{n+1}\le& 2\ell|\partial^* F\cap  W|+2\H^{n+1}(F\setminus E_t)\ &+2\ell \int_{W\cap  F} P(
u)d\H^{n+1}. \end{split}\] Dividing by $\ell$ and letting $\ell	o \infty$ provides the required property.
nodes.statement_short: Test with $\wt F=(F\times(-\ell,\ell))\cup\wt E_t$ and let $\ell\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Proof that level sets agree with reduced boundaries
nodes.statement: This is proven exactly as \cite[Lemma 5.9]{S08}. Since $u\in C^{0,1}(\Omega)\subset \BV(\Omega)$ we can compare the coarea formula for BV-functions and Lipschitz functions to obtain \[\int_0^T\H^n(\partial^*E_t)dt=\int_{\Omega_1\cap\{u<T\}}|\nabla u|d\H^{n+1}=\int_0^T\H^n(\{u=t\})dt\] for any $T>0$, and thus \[\int_0^T\H^n(\{u=t\}\setminus\partial^* E_t)dt=0,\] which yields that $\H^n(\{u=t\}\setminus\partial^* E_t)=0$ for a.e. $t\in [0,T]$. Since this is true for all $T>0$, we obtain the result.
nodes.statement_short: Compare the BV and Lipschitz coarea formulas for $u$ and exhaust in $T$.

nodes.name: Compare the two coarea formulas
nodes.statement: This is proven exactly as \cite[Lemma 5.9]{S08}. Since $u\in C^{0,1}(\Omega)\subset \BV(\Omega)$ we can compare the coarea formula for BV-functions and Lipschitz functions to obtain \[\int_0^T\H^n(\partial^*E_t)dt=\int_{\Omega_1\cap\{u<T\}}|\nabla u|d\H^{n+1}=\int_0^T\H^n(\{u=t\})dt\] for any $T>0$, and thus \[\int_0^T\H^n(\{u=t\}\setminus\partial^* E_t)dt=0,\]
nodes.statement_short: For $u$ Lipschitz the BV and Lipschitz coarea formulas agree, forcing the difference to have zero integral.

nodes.name: Conclude for a.e. $t$ and all $T$
nodes.statement: which yields that $\H^n(\{u=t\}\setminus\partial^* E_t)=0$ for a.e. $t\in [0,T]$. Since this is true for all $T>0$, we obtain the result.
nodes.statement_short: A non-negative integrand with zero integral vanishes a.e.; exhaust in $T$.

nodes.name: Proof of the Radon measure convergence
nodes.statement:
The proof is almost identical to that of \cite[Proposition 5.10]{S08}. We go through the proof here pointing out the differences in our case. To fit our notation, one has to replace $i$, $\e_i$, $\Omega$, $E_t^i$, $N_t^i$, $E'_t$ and $\Gamma_t$ of \cite[Proposition 5.10]{S08} by $k$, $\e_k$, $\Omega_0$, $\wt E_t^k$, $\wt E_t$, $\wt \Sigma_t^k$ and $\Sigma_t$ respectively. Note first that, by Lemma~ef{bdrystar}, for almost every $t$ $\mu_t= \H^{n+1}es \wt \Sigma_t$, where recall that $\wt \Sigma_t=\partial \wt E_t=\Sigma_t	imes\R=\partial E_t	imes\R$. Fix a $t>0$, so that the above is true. By the minimizing property (Lemma~ef{emin}, Remark~ef{area bound}), $|\wt \Sigma^k_t|$ are locally uniformly bounded and thus, after passing to a subsequence, $\mu_t^k\stackrel{k	o\infty}{\longrightarrow}\mu$, where $\mu$ is a Radon measure in $\Omega_0	imes\R$ (note that here we keep the same notation for the subsequence, whereas in \cite[Proposition 5.10]{S08} the subsequence is denoted by $\{\mu_t^{i_j}\}_j\subset\{\mu_t^i\}_i$, so to fit our notation one has to further replace $i_j$ of \cite[Proposition 5.10]{S08} by $k$).\ { f Claim 1:} $\spt \mu\subset\{u=t\}	imes\R$.\ The proof of Claim 1 is identical to that of \cite[Claim 1 of proof of Proposition 5.10]{S08}.\ { f Claim 2:} For $B_(x)\subset\subset\Omega_0	imes\R$ \[\mu(\ov B_(x))\le \H^{n+1}(\partial B_(x))+C(K)\H^{n+2}(B_(x)).\] The proof of Claim 2 is the same as that of \cite[Claim 2 of proof of Proposition 5.10]{S08}, with the only difference being the bound for $\mu^{k}_t(B_(x))=\H^{n+1}(\partial^* \wt E_t^k\cap B_(x))$. In particular, here using Lemma~ef{emin} with $F= \wt E_t^k\cup B_(x)$, we obtain \[\mu^{k}_t(B_(x))+\int_{\wt E_t^k\cap B_(x)} P(
u_k)d\H^{n+2}\le  \H^{n+1}( \partial B_(x))+\int_{ B_(x)} P(
u_k)d\H^{n+2},\] which yields \[ \mu^{k}_t(B_(x))\le \H^{n+1}( \partial B_(x))+C(K)\H^{n+2}( B_(x)).\] We have then, as in \cite[Claim 2 of proof of Proposition 5.10]{S08}, that $\mu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the $\H^{n+1}$-measure (since the $\H^{n+2}$-measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the $\H^{n+1}$-measure). Thus, by the Radon-Nikodym theorem, Claim 1, and Lemma~ef{bdrystar}, we obtain that there exists a function $	heta\in L^\infty(\Sigma_t	imes\R, \H^{n+1})$ such that  egin{equation} \mu=(\H^{n+1}es(\partial^*E_t	imes\R))es	heta=\mu_tes	heta, \end{equation} where recall that $\Sigma_t=\partial E_t$. 
oindent{ f Claim 3:} $	heta\ge 1$ $\H^{n+1}$-a.e. on $\Sigma_t	imes\R$.\ The proof of Claim 3 is identical to that of \cite[Claim 3 of proof of Proposition 5.10]{S08}.\ { f Claim 4:} $	heta\le 1$ $\H^{n+1}$-a.e. on $\partial^*E_t$.\ The proof of Claim 4 is the same as that of \cite[Claim 4 of proof of Proposition 5.10]{S08} with the only difference being the way we obtain the bound for $\mu_\l^{k}(B_1)= \l^{-(n+2)}\mu_t^{k}(\l B_1)$ (denoted as $\mu_\l^{i_j}$ in \cite[line 20, page 221]{S08}). In particular, here, one has to use the minimizing property of $E_t^k$ given in Lemma~ef{emin} (whereas in \cite{S08} $E_t^k$ are minimizing area on the outside). This, however, does not change the argument as it only changes the bound by a term of order $\e$. More specifically, the term $\sup_{S_{2\e}\cap B_1}|P(
u_k)||S_{2\e}\cap B_1|$ should be added to the bound. Here, $P(
u_\k)$ is the term appearing in Lemma~ef{emin} and $S_{2\e}=\{x\in \R^{n+2}:|x_{n+2}|\le 2\e\}$ as in \cite{S08}. We remark also that in the proof of this claim, one uses ``rescalings'' of sets in $M	imes\R$ and of the measures $\mu_t^k, \mu_t$, which are defined via the exponential map. In particular one makes the identifications \[(B_(x), g)\simeq(B_(\vec 0), \exp^*_x g)\simeq (B_(0), \hat g_{ij}^\phi)\] as Riemannian manifolds, where $(B_(x), \phi)$ are the geodesic normal coordinates that correspond to the identification $(T_pM, g(p))\simeq(R^{n+2}, \langle\cdot,\cdotangle)$ as Hilbert spaces and $\hat g_{ij}^\phi=g_{ij}^\phi\circ\phi^{-1}$, where $\hat g_{ij}^\phi$ are the components of $g$ in geodesic normal coordinates. These identifications allow us to reduce the proof to the case that $M=\R^{n+1}$. We remark also that, since $\exp^{-1}$ is an isometry, the minimizing property given in Lemma~ef{emin} and Claim 2 (both of which are used in the proof of this claim) are preserved under these identifications. For a detailed discussion and proofs of these facts see \cite{Alex}. Finally, Claim 3 and Claim 4 imply that $	heta(x)=1$ $\H^{n+1}$-a.e. on $\Sigma_t	imes\R$. Thus, the limit measure $\mu$ does not depend on the subsequence and thus the whole sequence converges $\mu_t^k	o \mu_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Follow Schulze's Proposition 5.10 in four claims (support, density bound, $\theta\ge1$, $\theta\le1$) to identify the limit measure as the unit-density measure on $\Sigma_t\times\R$.

nodes.name: Notation and extraction of a converging subsequence
nodes.statement: The proof is almost identical to that of \cite[Proposition 5.10]{S08}. We go through the proof here pointing out the differences in our case. To fit our notation, one has to replace $i$, $\e_i$, $\Omega$, $E_t^i$, $N_t^i$, $E'_t$ and $\Gamma_t$ of \cite[Proposition 5.10]{S08} by $k$, $\e_k$, $\Omega_0$, $\wt E_t^k$, $\wt E_t$, $\wt \Sigma_t^k$ and $\Sigma_t$ respectively. Note first that, by Lemma~\ref{bdrystar}, for almost every $t$ $\mu_t= \H^{n+1}\res \wt \Sigma_t$, where recall that $\wt \Sigma_t=\partial \wt E_t=\Sigma_t\times\R=\partial E_t\times\R$. Fix a $t>0$, so that the above is true. By the minimizing property (Lemma~\ref{emin}, Remark~\ref{area bound}), $|\wt \Sigma^k_t|$ are locally uniformly bounded and thus, after passing to a subsequence, $\mu_t^k\stackrel{k\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}\mu$, where $\mu$ is a Radon measure in $\Omega_0\times\R$ (note that here we keep the same notation for the subsequence, whereas in \cite[Proposition 5.10]{S08} the subsequence is denoted by $\{\mu_t^{i_j}\}_j\subset\{\mu_t^i\}_i$, so to fit our notation one has to further replace $i_j$ of \cite[Proposition 5.10]{S08} by $k$).
nodes.statement_short: Match Schulze's notation and extract a Radon-measure limit $\mu$ using the uniform area bounds.

nodes.name: Claim 1: support of the limit measure
nodes.statement: {\bf Claim 1:} $\spt \mu\subset\{u=t\}\times\R$.\\ The proof of Claim 1 is identical to that of \cite[Claim 1 of proof of Proposition 5.10]{S08}.
nodes.statement_short: The support of $\mu$ is contained in $\{u=t\}\times\R$.

nodes.name: Claim 2: ball bound and Radon--Nikodym density
nodes.statement: {\bf Claim 2:} For $B_\r(x)\subset\subset\Omega_0\times\R$ \[\mu(\ov B_\r(x))\le \H^{n+1}(\partial B_\r(x))+C(K)\H^{n+2}(B_\r(x)).\] The proof of Claim 2 is the same as that of \cite[Claim 2 of proof of Proposition 5.10]{S08}, with the only difference being the bound for $\mu^{k}_t(B_\r(x))=\H^{n+1}(\partial^* \wt E_t^k\cap B_\r(x))$. In particular, here using Lemma~\ref{emin} with $F= \wt E_t^k\cup B_\r(x)$, we obtain \[\mu^{k}_t(B_\r(x))+\int_{\wt E_t^k\cap B_\r(x)} P(\nu_k)d\H^{n+2}\le  \H^{n+1}( \partial B_\r(x))+\int_{ B_\r(x)} P(\nu_k)d\H^{n+2},\] which yields \[ \mu^{k}_t(B_\r(x))\le \H^{n+1}( \partial B_\r(x))+C(K)\H^{n+2}( B_\r(x)).\] We have then, as in \cite[Claim 2 of proof of Proposition 5.10]{S08}, that $\mu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the $\H^{n+1}$-measure (since the $\H^{n+2}$-measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the $\H^{n+1}$-measure). Thus, by the Radon-Nikodym theorem, Claim 1, and Lemma~\ref{bdrystar}, we obtain that there exists a function $\theta\in L^\infty(\Sigma_t\times\R, \H^{n+1})$ such that \begin{equation} \mu=(\H^{n+1}\res(\partial^*E_t\times\R))\res\theta=\mu_t\res\theta, \end{equation} where recall that $\Sigma_t=\partial E_t$.
nodes.statement_short: A minimizing comparison with $F=\wt E_t^k\cup B_\rho(x)$ gives the ball bound, hence a density $\theta$.

nodes.name: Claim 3: $\theta\ge1$
nodes.statement: \noindent{\bf Claim 3:} $\theta\ge 1$ $\H^{n+1}$-a.e. on $\Sigma_t\times\R$.\\ The proof of Claim 3 is identical to that of \cite[Claim 3 of proof of Proposition 5.10]{S08}.
nodes.statement_short: Lower semicontinuity gives $\theta\ge1$ a.e.

nodes.name: Claim 4: $\theta\le1$
nodes.statement: {\bf Claim 4:} $\theta\le 1$ $\H^{n+1}$-a.e. on $\partial^*E_t$.\\ The proof of Claim 4 is the same as that of \cite[Claim 4 of proof of Proposition 5.10]{S08} with the only difference being the way we obtain the bound for $\mu_\l^{k}(B_1)= \l^{-(n+2)}\mu_t^{k}(\l B_1)$ (denoted as $\mu_\l^{i_j}$ in \cite[line 20, page 221]{S08}). In particular, here, one has to use the minimizing property of $E_t^k$ given in Lemma~\ref{emin} (whereas in \cite{S08} $E_t^k$ are minimizing area on the outside). This, however, does not change the argument as it only changes the bound by a term of order $\e$. More specifically, the term $\sup_{S_{2\e}\cap B_1}|P(\nu_k)||S_{2\e}\cap B_1|$ should be added to the bound. Here, $P(\nu_\k)$ is the term appearing in Lemma~\ref{emin} and $S_{2\e}=\{x\in \R^{n+2}:|x_{n+2}|\le 2\e\}$ as in \cite{S08}. We remark also that in the proof of this claim, one uses ``rescalings'' of sets in $M\times\R$ and of the measures $\mu_t^k, \mu_t$, which are defined via the exponential map. In particular one makes the identifications \[(B_\r(x), g)\simeq(B_\r(\vec 0), \exp^*_x g)\simeq (B_\r(0), \hat g_{ij}^\phi)\] as Riemannian manifolds, where $(B_\r(x), \phi)$ are the geodesic normal coordinates that correspond to the identification $(T_pM, g(p))\simeq(R^{n+2}, \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ as Hilbert spaces and $\hat g_{ij}^\phi=g_{ij}^\phi\circ\phi^{-1}$, where $\hat g_{ij}^\phi$ are the components of $g$ in geodesic normal coordinates. These identifications allow us to reduce the proof to the case that $M=\R^{n+1}$. We remark also that, since $\exp^{-1}$ is an isometry, the minimizing property given in Lemma~\ref{emin} and Claim 2 (both of which are used in the proof of this claim) are preserved under these identifications. For a detailed discussion and proofs of these facts see \cite{Alex}.
nodes.statement_short: Rescaling via the exponential map and the minimizing property give $\theta\le1$, with an extra $O(\e)$ term.

nodes.name: Conclude $\theta=1$ and convergence of the full sequence
nodes.statement: Finally, Claim 3 and Claim 4 imply that $\theta(x)=1$ $\H^{n+1}$-a.e. on $\Sigma_t\times\R$. Thus, the limit measure $\mu$ does not depend on the subsequence and thus the whole sequence converges $\mu_t^k\to \mu_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Claims 3 and 4 give $\theta=1$, so the limit is subsequence-independent.

nodes.name: Proof of the unit density of the limit measure
nodes.statement: The proof is exactly as in Claims 2-4 of the proof of Lemma~\ref{mainconvergence}, using now the measures $\H^n\res\partial^*E_\infty$ and $\mu_\infty\res\partial^*E_\infty$ (instead of $\mu_t$ and $\mu$, see \eqref{mumut}) and therefore we will not repeat it here. We point out that, to fit the notation of this lemma, one has to replace $\Omega_0, \mu_t^k, \wt E_t^k$ and $\nu_k$ (of Lemma~\ref{mainconvergence}) by $\Omega, \mu_{t_i}, E_{t_i}$ and $\nu$ respectively and also replace both $\Sigma_t$ and $\partial^*\wt E_t$ by $ \partial^* E_\infty$. We also remark that in the proof here we need to use Lemma~\ref{eminu} instead of Lemma~\ref{emin} (or rather its corollary given in Remark~\ref{minimrmk}) and the lower semicontinuity of finite perimeter sets (lower semicontinuity of BV functions) instead of that for Radon measures for the convergence $E_{t_i}\to E_\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat Claims 2-4 of Lemma \ref{mainconvergence} with the substitutions $\mu_t^k\to\mu_{t_i}$, $\wt E_t^k\to E_{t_i}$ and Lemma \ref{eminu} in place of Lemma \ref{emin}.
